Feature · The Polestar 1

Dying Star

Polestar has been shown the door in America. The car it named itself after is still here, still magnificent, and now costs less than a well-optioned pickup. A field guide to buying a unicorn with an expiry date.

By Diana Chambers · 28 minute read

I  ·  The bearing

The star that brought everyone home

Of all the stars overhead, one has done more for us than the rest put together — our own sun excepted. Polaris. The North Star. For centuries it was the thing that brought you back: by land, by sea, and eventually by air.

The trick is almost insultingly elegant. Measure the angle between Polaris and the horizon, and that angle is your latitude. Ten degrees above the horizon, ten degrees north of the equator. No computer, no satellite, no subscription. A sextant, a clear night and a steady hand, and the sky tells you where on Earth you are.

It isn't quite perfect, and the imperfection is worth knowing about, because it comes back later. Polaris does not sit on the celestial pole; it sits within about a degree of it and traces a tiny circle around it every night. Working navigators correct for that with almanac tables. Uncorrected, a raw sextant reading gets you within roughly sixty nautical miles — close enough to find a continent, not close enough to find a harbor.

Still. Celestial navigation may be the single greatest unlock in human history — the confidence to leave the sight of land, and everything downstream of it. All because a few people decided a fixed point of light was enough to gamble a ship on.

One footnote before we go anywhere. The Southern Hemisphere has no equivalent. There is a southern pole star — Sigma Octantis, a little over a degree from the south celestial pole — but at magnitude 5.42 it sits at the edge of naked-eye visibility and vanishes under a moon, a haze, or a lit deck. Southern navigators were never handed a guide star at all. Hold that thought.

And one more. NASA's summary of how stars end is the tidiest I've read: when a star runs out of fuel, gravity finally wins its long argument with internal pressure and the star collapses. What happens next depends entirely on how big it was. Ordinary stars shed their outer layers gently into a glowing cloud of gas. Massive ones detonate.

Remember which category is which. We are coming back for it.

II  ·  The rule

The paperwork that ended it

On June 25, 2026, Polestar — which took its name from Polaris, the guiding star — announced it was withdrawing from the United States. Not by choice. The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security had denied it authorization to sell new vehicles from the 2027 model year onward, and Polestar, to the surprise of approximately everyone, declined to fight it.

The instrument is the U.S. Connected Vehicle Rule, and it is not about where a car is bolted together. It is about what runs inside it and who could, in theory, be compelled to reach in. Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, cellular, satellite links, telematics: the rule targets vehicles whose connective tissue is designed or controlled by companies subject to the jurisdiction of China or Russia, on the reasoning that such companies may be compelled to hand over data or permit remote access.

Which is where Polestar gets caught. The brand presents as Swedish — Gothenburg headquarters, Swedish design language, a company that would very much like you to think of fjords. But Geely, the Chinese automotive giant, controls it.

And here is the twist that makes the whole thing feel less like policy and more like weather. Geely also owns Volvo. Volvo had what one report called constructive discussions with Commerce about governance, technology and data security — and kept its authorization for 2027. Same parent company. Different answer.

The strangest casualty is the Polestar 3, built in Ridgeville, South Carolina, in the same plant as the Volvo EX90 and on closely related bones. An American-built electric performance SUV, made by American workers, banned from sale in America. The rule reads straight past the factory gate and into the source code.

Plate I What the Connected Vehicle Rule actually reaches

Prohibited

  • Importing completed connected vehicles from model year 2027 onward that incorporate covered software
  • Selling those vehicles in the United States
  • Offering commercial services using vehicles with automated driving systems — robotaxi fleets and the like
  • Covered hardware, from model year 2030

Not touched

  • Your existing car. Anything built before model year 2027 is expressly grandfathered
  • Servicing, repairs and warranty work
  • Parts supply
  • Software updates to cars already sold
  • Resale — private, dealer or auction

Source: 15 CFR Part 791, Subpart D. Every prohibition in the rule attaches to importing or selling. The single services prohibition concerns automated driving systems, which the Polestar 1 does not have. Anyone telling you the regulation will brick the car in your garage is wrong on the law. The risks are commercial and physical, and we will get to them — but they are not this.

III  ·  Precedent

We have done this before, and we did it over chicken

It is never good news when one of the most technically adventurous car companies on Earth is pushed out of a market that likes it. But it is not new. In December 1963, Lyndon Johnson signed Proclamation 3564, and on January 7, 1964 the United States imposed a 25 percent tariff on four things: potato starch, dextrin, brandy, and light trucks.

The provocation was poultry. American industrial chicken farming had made American chicken so cheap that European producers panicked; France banned it outright, West Germany imposed price controls, and German farmers went around claiming the Americans were fattening birds with arsenic. By August 1962 the U.S. had lost a quarter of its European chicken sales. Diplomacy failed. Tariffs followed.

Three of those four tariffs have long since been lifted. Nobody remembers the brandy. The light-truck tariff is still here, sixty-two years later, and it is why an imported passenger car pays 2.5 percent and an imported pickup pays twenty-five.

It was never really about chicken either. White House tapes show Johnson needed the UAW's Walter Reuther to hold off a strike before the 1964 election; Reuther's price was that somebody do something about Volkswagen. The bill came due in vehicles — VW's Type 2 pickup, killed outright; Subaru welding rear-facing jump seats into the BRAT's bed so it would count as a car; and the Toyota Hilux, the default pickup of planet Earth, which Americans have simply never been allowed to buy.

Same machinery, new decade: a plausible national interest at the top of the memo, and at the bottom of it, a car you can't have.

IV  ·  The car

So go and find the lemonade

When the world hands you a trade regulation, you go looking for whatever just got cheaper. And what just got cheaper — dramatically, almost indecently cheaper — is the best car the company ever made.

The Polestar 1 was the first vehicle Polestar built, and it is a bonafide unicorn: a four-seat, carbon-bodied, 619-horsepower all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid grand tourer, capped at 1,500 units over three years, built in a purpose-tooled carbon-fiber facility in Chengdu, and discontinued in late 2021. Roughly 250 came to America. Nobody, including Polestar, will give you a firm number.

Chris Harris — the British journalist and racing driver, formerly of Top Gear, and about as hard to impress as the profession gets — bought one of these with his own money. He was told on delivery that his was the only Polestar 1 sold in the United Kingdom, which makes him the owner of what is arguably the rarest car in the country. That is the kind of endorsement no press fleet can manufacture.

Those numbers are worth sitting with, because they describe a car that shouldn't exist. In 2019, a supercharged and turbocharged four-cylinder driving the front wheels, two independent electric motors driving the rear, and a 34 kWh battery running down the spine of a carbon-fiber coupe was not a category. It was a dare.

V  ·  The shape

The best-sculpted thing Scandinavia has put on a road

Start with the fact that it is, essentially, a concept car that nobody watered down. The Volvo Concept Coupe of 2013 reached production almost unmolested — wide, low, with the long-hood proportions that made coupes worth wanting in the seventies and eighties, and without a single superfluous vent, crease, flare or chrome garnish to apologize for itself.

Its proportions are perfect, and it is very nearly a chameleon depending on where you stand. From the front it manages elegant and aggressive at the same time, which almost nothing does. From the side you get the magnificent simplicity of the silhouette. From behind, the hairs on your arms stand up.

One detail does more work than the rest of the body combined. There is a single line that picks up just ahead of the door handle and runs unbroken to the tail — a crease that reads like the top of a shoulder, a line of tension holding the whole rear of the car in shape. It is the only thing on the entire exterior that could be called a flourish, and once you have seen it you cannot stop seeing it.

People pulling alongside it cannot work out why they want to keep looking. But they do.The reliable verdict of anyone who has driven one

Underneath is the more interesting story. Every exterior panel is carbon-fiber-reinforced plastic — hood, trunk, doors, sides, roof structure — bonded to a modified Volvo SPA steel platform, with a bespoke carbon cross-member under the rear seats tying the floor to the trunk section, around sixty percent stiffer than steel. Polestar reckons the car would weigh roughly 500 pounds more without it.

It still weighs 5,170 pounds. To put that in perspective: a Jeep Grand Cherokee L Summit 4x4 weighs 5,068 pounds with the V6 and 5,279 with the V8. This two-door coupe sits neatly between the two engine options of a full-size three-row SUV. Carbon fiber did not make this car light. It made this car possible.

The result is a machine that has pulled off timelessness with a little hot-rod menace under the tailoring. It is the automotive equivalent of arriving at a race in black tie, holding an espresso, and running the limiter at 155.

VI  ·  Powertrain

The most complicated simple car ever built

Plate II Two axles, two energy sources, one very confused drivetrain

The party trick nobody mentions: the car changes drivetrain layout depending on its mood. In electric mode it is rear-wheel drive. Run the battery flat and travel on gasoline alone and it becomes a front-wheel-drive car. No other six-hundred-horsepower machine in history turns into a front-driver when you aren't paying attention.

The modes are where the thing gets genuinely clever, and where a one-day test drive will actively mislead you. There are three drive modes — Pure, Hybrid and Power — plus two functions layered on top that matter more than the modes do.

Hold freezes the battery where it is. Fifty miles of charge in the battery and a hundred and fifty miles of highway ahead? Hold means all fifty are still there when you arrive somewhere that deserves silence. Owners report using it constantly, and it is the single most sensible feature on the car. Charge does the opposite: it burns gasoline to refill the battery, which is thermodynamically ridiculous and occasionally exactly what you want, forty minutes out from a city center.

So the everyday shape of it is this. You leave in the morning in silence, on 232 horsepower and rear-wheel drive, and you are a good citizen. You spend the day not using a drop of fuel, because 52 electric miles covers more or less anybody's actual life. Then you hit the highway, the four-cylinder wakes up, and the whole thing detonates.

Car and Driver got 3.7 seconds to 60 and 11.9 seconds at 121 mph through the quarter. But the number that matters on a road is 30 to 50 mph in 1.9 seconds. That is not acceleration so much as a change of location: touch the throttle at any speed and the motors deliver instant, absurd shove while the engine is still deciding whether to get involved.

The noise is the honest failure, and nobody who has driven the car pretends otherwise. It is a twincharged 2.0-liter four working hard, and it sounds like exactly that — coarse where you want operatic, and conspicuously unmusical for a car that cost $156,500. Reviewers have been blunt about it. The counterargument, offered by people who bought one anyway, is that nobody chooses this car for its voice. You choose it because it is the cleverest thing in the class. But if you need your grand tourer to sing, stop reading now.

The chassis deserves its own paragraph because it is strange. Double wishbones up front; at the rear an integral-link arrangement with a transverse composite leaf spring — an old idea used for a very modern reason, because it gets the springs out of the way of a battery that needs the space. On top of that sit Öhlins DFV dampers with twenty-two manual settings, which you adjust with a wrench. Car and Driver noted you have to open the hood and jack the back up to reach them, and could not imagine an owner of a six-figure coupe bothering. Owners bother. The usual setup is soft for town, accepting that the body control goes a little vaguer at speed — a trade you get to make yourself, with a wrench, which is not a sentence anyone writes about a modern luxury car.

That is not a flaw. That is a car with an opinion, and a manufacturer that assumed you might have one too.

Stopping is handled by Akebono — six-piston monoblocs clamping 400 mm discs, from the supplier that did the McLaren P1's brakes — and 5,170 pounds disappears more calmly than it has any right to. And because each rear motor drives its own wheel through a planetary set, the torque vectoring is real rather than the braking-based imitation everyone else was selling. Push hard and the tail starts to participate: controllable, never nervous, and a standing reminder of where the mass lives.

VII  ·  Range

How far it actually goes

Here is where I have to spoil a good line, including one of my own. The romance of this car is that you can cross a country in it without ever thinking about a charger — and that is true. But the specific claims people make about it, mine included, deserve a tape measure.

The arithmetic: 52 miles of EPA electric range, a 15.9-gallon tank, and — on gasoline alone — 26 mpg combined, 22 in the city, 31 on the highway. Which means the honest answer to "how far will it go" is a range, not a number. Driven normally: about 465 miles. Driven gently on an interstate at the EPA highway figure: about 545.

Plate III How far it reaches — road distance on true bearing

How to read it: each city sits at its true compass bearing from the origin, at a radius equal to its approximate road distance — not straight-line distance, because a car cannot fly. The outer magenta ring is 465 miles, the realistic one-way reach on a full tank and a full charge. The inner blue ring is 232 miles — the farthest you can go and still get home again without stopping. Note where Las Vegas falls between the two. Driven gently at the EPA highway figure, that outer ring stretches to roughly 545.

So let's settle the famous one. Los Angeles to Las Vegas is 270 miles up I-15, which the car eats without noticing — a bit over half a tank, with the electric miles quietly spent in traffic before you clear San Bernardino. The round trip is 540 miles, and that is where it gets interesting, because 540 lands almost exactly in the gap between the car's two honest range figures. At the EPA combined rate you come up about seventy-five miles short somewhere around Barstow. Drive it the way you actually drive a grand tourer on an empty desert interstate — steady, top gear, the four-cylinder loafing — and the highway figure puts you home with fuel to spare.

So it is a genuine coin flip, decided entirely by your right foot. Which is why the smart move is the obvious one: plug in overnight at the hotel, as every garage on the Strip now permits, take back your 52 electric miles for roughly the price of a bad cocktail, and remove the question altogether. You will have driven to Las Vegas and back without once standing at a pump in Baker, and you can decide for yourself whether that counts as one tank.

Europe is where the car makes more sense than anywhere. Four hundred and seventy miles from Paris covers Amsterdam, Brussels, Lyon, Geneva, Frankfurt, Zurich and Bordeaux. Bordeaux at 360 miles means you arrive with a hundred and ten in hand and can do the last stretch into the city in complete silence. Barcelona at 640 needs one splash of fuel. Madrid needs two. Not a bad range for a car you can also take to the shops without waking the neighbors.

European owners report much the same shape to it — around eighty miles of usable electric range against an official WLTP figure of 77, then roughly 350 more on gasoline. Serious grand-touring legs, in other words, and that is the actual point of this car. It is not a fast EV and it is not a quick gasoline coupe. It is the only vehicle of its era that genuinely did both jobs without asking you to plan your life around it.

VIII  ·  The cabin

Cocooned, and slightly sunburned

Inside, you are in command of it in a way that modern cars have largely forgotten how to arrange. The seats hold you the way a mother holds a child on the first day of school — firm, reluctant to let go, and considerably more comfortable than that metaphor implies. They are the single best thing about being in the car.

The rest is clean and minimalist without tipping into stark. There is a vertically oriented touchscreen angled toward the driver, a 12.3-inch digital cluster, a head-up display, and — crucially — enough physical switchgear left in place that you are not hunting through menus to change the temperature. It is the balance between screen and button that everybody has spent the last five years getting wrong, and that this car, in 2019, simply got right.

Now the honest part, because it is the most-repeated criticism of the car. This is a Volvo cabin. The instrument panel, steering wheel and infotainment came out of the S90 and V90 with a badge swap and a change of trim. Every reviewer noticed, and the comparison that kept getting made was to a Bentley Continental, which does feel more special in there. The rebuttal is simply that you are paying for what is underneath rather than for wood veneer and a clock made by a watch brand — and given what is underneath this particular car, that is a defensible trade.

What is genuinely bespoke is the material story: carbon fiber and chrome across the dash, leather stitched with real care, a crystal gearshift, a Bowers & Wilkins system, and — my favorite detail on the whole car — a transparent panel in the trunk showing the battery electronics underneath. It is a car visibly proud of its own plumbing.

Where it gets caught out is the small stuff a $156,500 car should not get caught out on. No power adjustment for the steering column. No powered thigh extensions. And the big one: an enormous fixed glass roof with no shade of any kind. Glorious in Gothenburg. Below the 45th parallel you are being slowly and thoroughly roasted, and it is the one design decision on the entire car that feels like it was signed off by someone who had never left Sweden.

IX  ·  The catch

What it isn't

Not everything here is wonderful. The rear seats are an over-simplification of the concept of rear seats. Anyone over four feet should be encouraged to take the train, unless you are immune to complaining. Small children fit, and hunch. This is a grand touring coupe with occasional room for family, or for somebody else's family, and it should be sold as such.

The trunk is 4.4 cubic feet, because a battery lives in it. In practical terms that is not quite three airline carry-ons. It will take a few bags for a long weekend, or the food for that weekend, but not both, and under no circumstances should this car be taken to Costco.

And it has never been crash-tested by NHTSA, the IIHS or Euro NCAP. Not because it failed anything, but because none of them will buy and destroy a car this rare. It carries Volvo's full active safety suite — automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection, lane-keeping, blind-spot monitoring, a 360-degree camera, and Pilot Assist adaptive cruise with lane centering — from a company whose entire reputation is built on not killing you. But there is no independent number, and you should know that.

X  ·  The money

The price of a fallen star

Before any of this happened, a used Polestar 1 was still a six-figure car. Rarity, capability, and the particular devotion of the people who owned them held the price up. Then the floor went.

Note the date on the cheapest one. The $46,500 sale — the lowest verified Polestar 1 transaction on record — closed on June 15, 2026, ten days before the ban was announced. It cannot be a reaction to it.

That last point matters, because the easy story is wrong. The curve was already falling: $83,000 in 2022, $67,500 in 2024, $62,500 in 2025. This is what happens to a 1,500-unit orphan plug-in hybrid coupe from a brand with no badge equity, and it was happening steadily before Washington said a word. The ban is a headline draped over a trend that was already in progress.

What did move is the brand. Polestar as a whole is down roughly 7.9 percent in thirty days on CarGurus against a market that moved a fraction of a percent — but that figure is dominated by the Polestar 2, not the 1. And a Final Edition, one of only twenty-five built, failed to sell at Barrett-Jackson Scottsdale in January.

Where that leaves you today: realistic asking prices run $50,000 to $75,000. Delivery-mileage collector examples are being advertised at $89,800 to $103,000, and none of them have sold at those numbers. And Polestar's own Boston store still has a two-thousand-mile car listed at $156,500 — the original sticker, six years later — which is either the most optimistic listing in America or a spreadsheet nobody has opened since 2021.

So on average, around sixty thousand dollars. That is Aston Martin depreciation, the kind that used to happen before you had finished the paperwork. And it buys a carbon-fiber, 619-horsepower, 3.7-second grand tourer that a few hundred people in this country own.

Which is only half the point. The other half is what else sixty thousand dollars buys, because the Polestar 1 did not exist in a vacuum. It launched into a very specific moment — the last gasp of the big two-door grand tourer, when every luxury manufacturer was placing its bet on what a fast coupe would look like after gasoline. Line them all up today and something remarkable happens.

Read that chart again, because it is the entire argument of this piece compressed into five bars.

The Polestar 1 cost more than the i8, more than the M8, and nearly as much as an NSX. It out-powers the i8 by 250 horsepower. It has almost three times the i8's electric range and infinitely more than the other three, none of which have a plug at all. The Lexus is a lovely thing that cannot get out of its own way. The M8 is savagely fast and drinks like it. The NSX is the one everybody agreed was the future, and it has held 88 percent of its value, which is wonderful for the people who own one and useless to you.

And the Polestar — the rarest of the five by a factor of two, the only one you can genuinely drive all week without burning a drop of gasoline, the one with the carbon body and the Öhlins and the two motors doing real torque vectoring — is the cheapest thing on the list. By a distance.

Price is only half of it, though. Put the same five cars on a stopwatch, a scale and a fuel pump and the picture gets stranger still.

Plate VI Six measurements, five cars

0–60 figures are Edmunds' instrumented tests — one publication, one protocol, all five cars — so they compare cleanly even though Car and Driver recorded 3.7 seconds for the Polestar 1. Quarter-mile times are Car and Driver's, except the i8's, which is MotorTrend's. Trap speeds, in order: 121, 112, 103, 129 and 126 mph. Nobody published a 60–0 figure for the i8 or the LC 500h, so those cells are blank rather than guessed — but note what the three verified numbers say: the heaviest car here stops shortest.

The Polestar is the heaviest thing here by some margin — nearly 900 pounds more than the M8, and almost 1,700 more than the i8 — and it does not matter nearly as much as it should. It runs the quarter mile quicker than the i8 and the Lexus combined could manage on a good day. It returns better fuel economy than the M8 and the NSX while carrying the most power of any hybrid in the group. And in the one test where all that mass ought to punish it savagely, it stops in 99 feet: shorter than the M8, shorter than the NSX, shorter than anything else here that anyone bothered to measure.

Every other car here is priced according to what the market decided it was. The Polestar is priced according to a mistake.The reason the timing is now

XI  ·  Ownership

The three things you actually need to know

Buying an orphan is a real fear and it deserves a real answer, so here it is, briefly, because the point of this car is not its service schedule.

One: Volvo did not leave. This is the whole ballgame. The Polestar 1 sits on Volvo's SPA platform, uses an engine derived from the XC90 T8, runs Volvo's Sensus software, and is diagnosable with Volvo's own tools. Polestar's U.S. service centers already live physically inside Volvo dealerships — and Volvo, same Geely parent, kept its authorization. Whatever becomes of Polestar's American entity, the dealer network, the parts logistics and the technicians this car depends on are staying exactly where they are. Not every Volvo store is Polestar-certified, so call one before you buy rather than after.

Two: the regulation cannot touch your car, and it never could. The rule bans importing and selling. It says nothing about servicing, parts, warranty work or resale, and anything built before model year 2027 is expressly grandfathered. As a bonus, the Polestar 1 never received over-the-air updates in the first place — it's a Sensus car, updated at a service bay — so the software panic filling the coverage is about the 2, 3 and 4, not this.

Three: the clock that matters is the battery warranty, not the Commerce Department. Eight years or 100,000 miles on the high-voltage pack and motors; ten and 150,000 in California. A 2020 car runs to roughly 2028, a 2021 to 2029. Buy inside that window. Run a VIN check for the 2023 battery recall and the 2024 brake-pedal recall while you're at it — both were fixed free, and the battery remedy was a complete pack replacement, which is quietly reassuring news about whether packs exist.

The genuine risk is the carbon. Every panel and the roof structure came from a plant in Chengdu that no longer builds the car, there is no aftermarket, and a serious shunt very likely totals it. So insure it properly and accept that you are custodian of something fragile and finite.

That's it. That's the homework. Everything else about this car is upside.

XII  ·  Method

Navigating without the North Star

So, like sailors and navigators before us, we will have to rely on something other than the North Star. Which turns out to be the least original problem in human history, because here is the thing that every serious navigator knew and that the rest of us have quietly forgotten:

The North Star was always temporary.

The Earth wobbles. Not much, and not quickly, but relentlessly — the axis traces a slow circle against the sky, one full revolution every 25,772 years, drifting about a degree every seventy-two. The pole star is not a fixture. It is just whatever bright thing happens to be standing near the pole when you look up.

Plate VII The relay of pole stars · one full precession cycle

Bands show tenure where it is well defined; markers show each star's closest approach to the pole. The job has changed hands repeatedly, and it will keep changing hands — roughly one degree of drift every seventy-two years.

When the Egyptians were stacking the pyramids, north was Thuban, in Draco. And Thuban was a better pole star than Polaris has ever been, sitting within ten arcminutes of true north around 2830 BC. It was also magnitude 3.65 — dim enough that you had to know where to look. Then Kochab took a turn. Polaris only inherited the job comparatively recently, and it reaches its own closest approach around AD 2100, at twenty-seven arcminutes. That is Polaris at its very best, and it is still not quite on the mark.

After that it drifts off, and the plate above has the rest of the relay. Every navigator who ever steered by the North Star was using a temporary arrangement, and almost none of them knew it.

And south of the equator, as I mentioned at the start, they never had one at all. So southern navigators were not given a star. They were given a problem, and they solved it with a method: take the long axis of the Southern Cross, from Gacrux through Acrux, extend it four and a half times its own length, and there is the pole. Cross-check it with a perpendicular dropped from the midpoint between Alpha and Beta Centauri. Two lines, one intersection, and an empty patch of sky that is nonetheless exactly where south is.

They didn't have a landmark. They had a technique. And the technique worked in every weather the landmark did, plus a few it didn't.The southern solution

That is the whole lesson, and it is the lesson here too. You do not actually need the star. You need the bearing.

Because the idea inside this car is not leaving America. A six-hundred-horsepower coupe that runs silent through a city and crosses a continent without a moment's anxiety was a very strange proposition in 2019. It is now simply how fast cars are built.

Look at what the establishment did next. The current BMW M5 is a plug-in hybrid — not the next one, the one in showrooms right now: 717 horsepower, a V8 with a motor in the transmission, 25 miles of electric range, and a curb weight of about 5,390 pounds, which is to say it is heavier than the Polestar 1 that everybody called a fat compromise. The current Mercedes-AMG C63 is a plug-in hybrid four-cylinder — 671 horsepower out of a two-liter four with an electrically spun turbo and a motor on the rear axle, a decision people found scandalous when it landed and which this car had quietly made years earlier. Its EPA electric range is one mile. One. The Polestar 1 does fifty-two.

Then look further up. The Ferrari SF90 puts electric motors on the front axle and a V8 behind you. The Lamborghini Revuelto does the same thing with a V12. And Chevrolet's new ZR1X runs an electric front axle and a twin-turbo V8 rear axle with no mechanical connection between them at all — which is, structurally, the exact architecture a Swedish coupe shipped in 2019 for a third of the money.

Three or four years after this thing launched, everybody was building one. Volvo and Polestar were not just first. They were first, and they were right, and almost nobody noticed at the time — which is precisely why you can now buy the thing for the price of a mid-spec pickup.

Polestar took the bearing, sailed it, proved it was correct, and then got shown the door for reasons that have nothing whatever to do with the engineering.

XIII  ·  Full circle

The dying star

Here is where the obvious assumption turns out to be wrong, and the correction makes the whole metaphor better.

Polaris is a supergiant. Spectral class F7Ib, about 446 light years away, the brightest member of a triple system, roughly 1,260 times as luminous as our sun and forty-six times as wide. It is also a Cepheid variable, which means it physically swells and contracts on a cycle of just under four days — a star that breathes.

And that word "supergiant" makes everybody assume it goes out in a supernova. It does not. Core collapse requires something on the order of eight solar masses. In 2024, interferometry at the CHARA Array measured Polaris directly and got 5.13, give or take 0.28. It is not close. It is not even in the conversation.

So Polaris will do exactly what NASA said ordinary stars do. It will swell out onto the asymptotic giant branch, and then it will exhale — a slow superwind pushing its outer layers off into a glowing shell of gas, a planetary nebula lit from the inside, and at the center a naked, cooling ember about the size of the Earth. A white dwarf. Not a bang. A long, luminous breath out, and then a light that fades for billions of years without ever quite going away.

Which is more or less what has happened here. Polestar did not explode. It issued a press release, kept its European business, and left. What it leaves behind is the bright part: a few hundred carbon-bodied coupes scattered across America, still running, still gorgeous, still far faster than they have any business being — cooling slowly, and visible for a long time yet.

One last thing about Polaris, because it is too good to leave out. Something odd happened to it in the last century. Its pulsation collapsed after 1966, almost to nothing, and astronomers assumed it was quietly switching itself off. Then it started up again — the only Cepheid ever observed to reverse. And compared to what Ptolemy wrote down, Polaris today is around two and a half times brighter than it was.

Dying stars do not always behave themselves. Occasionally they come back. If you want to keep hoping Polestar returns to America, you have astronomical precedent on your side.

XIV  ·  The verdict

So. Sixty-forty.

Plate VIII The dilemma, weighted
60 · Buy it
40 · Don't

Sixty says yes

  • Sixty thousand dollars buys a carbon-fiber, 619 hp, 3.7-second grand tourer of which a couple of hundred exist in this country. There is no other answer to that sentence.
  • The mechanical core is Volvo, and Volvo is staying.
  • The design has not dated and shows no sign of starting.
  • The depreciation already happened — to somebody else. The cliff is behind you.
  • The regulation does not touch a car already in your garage.
  • Nothing else does both jobs. Silent city, effortless continent, one car.

Forty says no

  • The high-voltage warranty expires in 2028 or 2029, and no replacement price has ever been published.
  • A carbon panel from a shuttered Chinese plant is a problem money cannot solve quickly.
  • The service commitment is a promise with no stated duration, from a company that just lost its reason to be here.
  • It is still a car that shares a great deal with a Volvo costing a third as much, and your rear-seat passengers will bring it up.
  • Values have not stopped falling.

The tiebreaker is what you think you are buying. Buy it as an asset and the forty percent will eat you: you will spend six years refreshing auction results, flinching at every recall notice, and treating a magnificent car like a stock you cannot sell.

Buy it as a car and the calculation changes completely. Get a VIN check on all three recalls. Buy one still inside the high-voltage warranty, which most of them are. Live somewhere within reach of a Polestar-certified Volvo dealer. Put it on an agreed-value policy. And then drive it, which is the entire point and the thing almost nobody who owns one seems willing to do.

Do that, and the forty percent becomes weather. Unpleasant, occasionally expensive, and survivable.

Because in twenty years, when somebody asks what the strangest, prettiest, most quietly ambitious car of the whole electrification panic actually was, the answer is going to be a Swedish carbon-fiber coupe with a supercharged and turbocharged four up front, two electric motors out back, a Chinese parent, an American factory it never got to use, and a name borrowed from a star that is, at this exact moment, slowly and rather beautifully going out.

Go and look at one. Preferably at night.
